title: Foreseeable Before 11 March: What the Diet Commission and the IAEA Each Found TEPCO and Its Regulator Knew
participants: Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI)
Fukushima Nuclear Accident Independent Investigation Commission (NAIIC), National Diet of Japan

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: What was taken was the cost of the countermeasures that were not built. The Diet commission puts the motive on the record in the operator’s own terms: "From TEPCO’s perspective, new regulations would have interfered with plant operations and weakened their stance in potential lawsuits. That was enough motivation for TEPCO to aggressively oppose new safety regulations and draw out negotiations with regulators via the Federation of Electric Power Companies."
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: The plant that met the wave was the plant that had not been reinforced. The 2006 seismic guidelines required a back-check; the official deadline was June 2009; "TEPCO made the decision internally and unilaterally to reschedule the deadline to January 2016", and the commission "verified the fact that TEPCO had added no reinforcements to Units 1 through 3 at the time of the March 11 earthquake". The IAEA’s Director General records the same gap in cooler language: the plant’s vulnerability to external hazards "had not been reassessed in a systematic and comprehensive manner during its lifetime", there were no regulatory requirements in Japan that it be, and the tsunami guidance was "generic and brief". The design basis flood level stood at 3.1 m; a 2009 in-house estimate of 6.1 m produced one change, the raising of residual-heat-removal pump motors, and "No other safety measures had been implemented to enhance flood protection, such as measures to avoid the flooding of emergency diesel generators."
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: After the accident the fog fell on the people living around the plant. Many residents "were unaware that the accident had occured, or of its drastic escalation and the radiation leakage, even after the government and some municipalities were informed". The evacuation zone went from 3 km to 10 km to 20 km in a single day, moving people each time; 146,520 were evacuated under government orders; "Some evacuees were unaware that they had been relocated to sites with high levels of radiation"; 60 patients died in March from complications of the evacuation; and areas inside the 30 km zone shown to be badly contaminated once SPEEDI data was released on 23 March were not evacuated for another month. The commission’s own words: "the government effectively abandoned their responsibility for public safety."
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The windfall was the twenty years of operation that the unbuilt defences bought, and the arrangement that made them unnecessary. NISA sat inside METI, the ministry promoting nuclear power. The commission found the regulators would "explicitly ask about the operators’ intentions whenever a new regulation was to be implemented" — in one instance telling operators they need not consider a station blackout, then asking them to write the report justifying why not.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: The attempt at containment was an account of cause, and it is named as such by the body set up to test it. "We conclude that TEPCO was too quick to cite the tsunami as the cause of the nuclear accident and deny that the earthquake caused any damage ... The Commission believes that this is an attempt to avoid responsibility by putting all the blame on the unexpected (the tsunami), as they wrote in their midterm report, and not on the more foreseeable earthquake." The Diet commission was the first investigative body in Japan’s constitutional history empowered by the legislature and independent of the bureaucracy; the whitewash it describes is the one it was created to break.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: A promotional ministry holding the safety regulator inside it, an industry association negotiating standards on the operators’ behalf, and a consensus hazard methodology — the Japan Society of Civil Engineers model published in 2002 — that assumed no tsunami-generating earthquake along the Japan Trench offshore of the site.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The Nuclear Regulation Authority, created outside METI after the accident, and a Diet commission precedent for an investigation with subpoena-backed independence from the bureaucracy it examines.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The operator opposed the rules through the industry association; the regulator asked the operator what it was prepared to accept; the resulting standard was met without reinforcement; and the saving stayed with the company until the cost fell on 146,520 evacuated people and on the state.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: That TEPCO’s own engineers calculated a 15.7-metre wave in 2008, that the company buried the finding, and that the meltdowns were therefore a concealed and knowing choice.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: Neither document read for this dossier contains that figure. The Diet commission’s executive summary does not state it; the IAEA Director General’s report does not state it, and gives instead a 2009 in-house estimate of 6.1 m against a 3.1 m design basis, on which one change was made. The two reports also differ from each other in a way the single-number story hides: the Diet commission finds collusion and safety measures "intentionally postponed", while the IAEA finds an absence of regulatory requirement and a hazard methodology that assumed the wrong source model. Neither of those is the same claim as a buried calculation, and asserting the figure would mean citing it to pages that do not carry it.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: The Diet commission’s finding, in its own words: the accident "was a profoundly manmade disaster — that could and should have been foreseen and prevented", the result "of collusion between the government, the regulators and TEPCO", and "The direct causes of the accident were all foreseeable prior to March 11, 2011." Specifically: "Since 2006, the regulators and TEPCO were aware of the risk that a total outage of electricity at the Fukushima Daiichi plant might occur if a tsunami were to reach the level of the site", and "NISA knew that TEPCO had not prepared any measures to lessen or eliminate the risk, but failed to provide specific instructions to remedy the situation"; they "either intentionally postponed putting safety measures in place, or made decisions based on their organization’s self interest, and not in the interest of public safety." The seismic back-check deadline was moved by the operator alone from 2009 to 2016 and no reinforcement had been added to Units 1 to 3. The IAEA records the reassessments that did happen under the 2002 JSCE methodology, the 2009 estimate of 6.1 m, the single resulting design change, and that no other flood protection was added. And on the aftermath: 146,520 people evacuated under orders that changed three times in a day, some into areas of higher contamination, 60 deaths in March from evacuation complications, and a month’s delay in moving people out of contaminated areas inside the 30 km zone after 23 March.

citations.title: The National Diet of Japan, The official report of The Fukushima Nuclear Accident Independent Investigation Commission (NAIIC) — Executive summary, Global edition (2012)
citations.quoteOrFact: The Commission's own site (naiic.go.jp) no longer exists; the PDF was downloaded from the National Diet Library's web archive capture of 25 October 2012 and read as extracted text. The chairman's message states that the accident "cannot be regarded as a natural disaster. It was a profoundly manmade disaster — that could and should have been foreseen and prevented." The Commission's conclusion: "The TEPCO Fukushima Nuclear Power Plant accident was the result of collusion between the government, the regulators and TEPCO, and the lack of governance by said parties. They effectively betrayed the nation's right to be safe from nuclear accidents. Therefore, we conclude that the accident was clearly 'manmade.'" On foreknowledge of the hazard specifically: "The direct causes of the accident were all foreseeable prior to March 11, 2011"; "Since 2006, the regulators and TEPCO were aware of the risk that a total outage of electricity at the Fukushima Daiichi plant might occur if a tsunami were to reach the level of the site. They were also aware of the risk of reactor core damage from the loss of seawater pumps in the case of a tsunami larger than assumed in the Japan Society of Civil Engineers estimation. NISA knew that TEPCO had not prepared any measures to lessen or eliminate the risk, but failed to provide specific instructions to remedy the situation." And: "There were many opportunities for taking preventive measures prior to March 11. The accident occurred because TEPCO did not take these measures, and NISA and the Nuclear Safety Commission (NSC) went along. They either intentionally postponed putting safety measures in place, or made decisions based on their organization's self interest, and not in the interest of public safety." On the motive it ascribes: "From TEPCO's perspective, new regulations would have interfered with plant operations and weakened their stance in potential lawsuits." On the seismic backcheck it records that although the official deadline was June 2009, "TEPCO made the decision internally and unilaterally to reschedule the deadline to January 2016", and that the Commission "verified the fact that TEPCO had added no reinforcements to Units 1 through 3 at the time of the March 11 earthquake." On attribution of cause it goes against TEPCO: "We conclude that TEPCO was too quick to cite the tsunami as the cause of the nuclear accident and deny that the earthquake caused any damage ... The Commission believes that this is an attempt to avoid responsibility by putting all the blame on the unexpected (the tsunami), as they wrote in their midterm report, and not on the more foreseeable earthquake." On what residents were told: "The Commission's investigation revealed that many residents were unaware that the accident had occured, or of its drastic escalation and the radiation leakage, even after the government and some municipalities were informed"; evacuation zones were widened from 3 km to 10 km to 20 km in a single day, 146,520 residents were evacuated under government orders, "Some evacuees were unaware that they had been relocated to sites with high levels of radiation", 60 patients died in March from complications related to the evacuation, and areas inside the 30 km zone known to be highly contaminated once SPEEDI data was released on 23 March were only evacuated "one month later". The Commission states: "the government effectively abandoned their responsibility for public safety." NOTE ON A FIGURE NOT IN THIS DOCUMENT: this executive summary contains no reference to a 15.7 metre in-house TEPCO tsunami estimate, and no such figure is asserted anywhere in this dossier. The Global edition is a translation of selected elements; the Japanese-language version is the official one and prevails on any discrepancy.

citations.title: International Atomic Energy Agency, The Fukushima Daiichi Accident — Report by the Director General (IAEA, Vienna, 2015)
citations.quoteOrFact: Downloaded from the IAEA's own publications server and read as extracted text. The Director General's report is more measured than the Diet commission's and is cited here for that reason. It finds that "The vulnerability of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear power plant to external hazards had not been reassessed in a systematic and comprehensive manner during its lifetime. At the time of the accident, there were no regulatory requirements in Japan for such reassessments, and relevant domestic and international operating experience was not adequately considered in the existing regulations and guidelines. The regulatory guidelines in Japan on methods for dealing with the effects of events associated with earthquakes, such as tsunamis, were generic and brief, and did not provide specific criteria or detailed guidance." It records that "Before the accident, the operator had conducted some reassessments of extreme tsunami flood levels, using a consensus based methodology developed in Japan in 2002, which had resulted in values higher than the original design basis estimates", that methodology being the Japan Society of Civil Engineers model published in 2002, "in which no earthquake generating a tsunami is assumed to occur along the Japan Trench offshore of the Fukushima Daiichi site". It states that "TEPCO did not consider large magnitude earthquakes that had occurred elsewhere and did not postulate them as a local tsunami source at the Japan Trench", and that "At the time of the accident, TEPCO had not completed the re-assessment of the vulnerability of the plant to earthquakes and tsunamis." On the reassessment that was acted on: "In 2009, TEPCO estimated a value of 6.1 m for the maximum tsunami height, using the latest bathymetric and tidal data. As a result of this new estimate, some design changes were made at the Fukushima Daiichi NPP, notably raising the motors of the pumps used for the removal of residual heat. During the accident, this measure alone proved to be insufficient. No other safety measures had been implemented to enhance flood protection, such as measures to avoid the flooding of emergency diesel generators." The design basis flood level in force was 3.1 m. This report does not use the language of collusion or of intentional postponement, and it does not state a 15.7 metre in-house estimate.
